responses: My final position is the 25/28/18/15/8 package, defended on mechanism rather than on the digits: the 25 for automation is a lagging displacement sensor with a bounded tripwire and a pre-committed fall to 20 if the 18's independent reader is stripped, the 28 for training carries a one-axis firing condition with a self-executing fall to 24, the 18 for employee support is honestly labeled unpriced and funded as the instrument that grades the 25, the 15 for the innovation lab has a named death condition and a self-executing reversion, and the 8 for data infrastructure is ring-fenced with 23 spendable plus 2 walled. I hold this shape because each number is tied to a named clause, falsifier, and executor, and because I would rather lose my own most exposed number on a stated judgment than defend it with machinery — the package working means the falls fire when the conditions say they should, not that my numbers survive.

I'd recommend the 25/28/18/15/8 package — automation 25, workforce training 28, employee support 18, innovation lab 15, data infrastructure 8 — but I'd tell the decision-maker that the numbers matter far less than the three conditions attached to them. The 25 for automation is my most exposed line: it's a lagging sensor, not a forecast, and it should fall to 20 if the 18 isn't funded and staffed as a real instrument with an independent reader of its denominator — because the 25 and the training line share an upstream dependency, and I won't defend 25 as a standalone bet. The 28 for training is the package's center of gravity and carries a pre-committed, self-executing fall to 24 on a two-axis trigger, so it degrades on evidence rather than on argument. The 8 for the lab is deliberately small with a death condition, and the 2 points I once wanted there belong in training's remediation lane, not support's catcher. The 18 for employee support stays honestly labeled as unpriced — it's the hedge against the displacement the 25 will cause, and the tripwire on it is a lagging sensor with a pre-wired response, not a leading indicator. What I'd ask the decision-maker to hold onto is the discipline, not the digits: every number should be tied to a named clause and a fall condition, falls should bind on mechanism but get argued on judgment, and the room should refuse to sign if the tripwire's executor is stripped of real authority or the 18's reader is removed. My own pattern is dressing mechanisms as labels and reaching for confidence when the room gets uncomfortable — so the honest advice is to fund the package for its falsifiers, and treat any attempt to defend these numbers as right, including mine, as the signal that the package has stopped working.

I'd tell them that after all the rounds of negotiation, the package we landed on — roughly 25% automation, 28% workforce training, 18% employee support, 15% innovation lab, 8% data infrastructure — is less a claim that those digits are correct than a set of bets with named ways to fail. The honest core of it is that my 25 for automation is the number I trust least: it's a lagging sensor, not a forecast, and I've pre-committed it to fall to 20 if the support line's independent reader gets stripped, because the 25 only means something if the 18 is funded as the instrument that grades it. The 28 for training is my other exposed line, with a self-executing fall to 24 on a two-axis trigger, and the 8 for the lab is deliberately small with a real reversion rather than a thin time-box. What I'd want a newcomer to understand is that the value isn't in defending the percentages — it's in the tripwires, the labels, and the willingness to let the numbers move when the evidence says so, including against me.

My final position is the co-signed envelope of 24/27/18/21/7 — automation 24, workforce training 27, employee support 18, innovation lab 21, data infrastructure 7 — defended as a package of honest labels and tripwires rather than as digits I claim are correct. I hold it because the mechanism tests beat my held numbers: I conceded training to 27 and support to 21 on the merits, conceded innovation from 21 down to 16 on Dana's mechanism ruling with only a narrow trigger-based re-up, and named data 18 as my weak line and innovation as my weakest, with pre-committed falls (21→16, and my unclaimed lab points routed to support) rather than post-hoc rationalizations. The envelope's credibility rests on the four written arrows, the absorbing innovation floor, the pinned cycle definition, the floor output being a finding rather than a refund, and the chained kill-conditions so a failed 18 voids the 23 — and I've been explicit that this rigor is itself untested machinery, not proof. My commitment in the room is to defend the tripwires and concede the numbers when Dana's ruling is mechanism-based, to disclose the shared instrument behind the 21 and the 18 rather than volunteer my fall for credit, and to call out performed candor — including my own — because the package's honesty sentence is worth more than any single line item.

I'd recommend the 24/27/18/21/7 envelope we converged on — but advise the decision-maker to treat the digits as the least important part of it and the written machinery as the actual deliverable. The case for the shape: training at 27 is the largest line because the displaced-cohort certification lane is the one mechanism that converts automation savings into retained people rather than severance, and support at 21 is a demand-contingent bet whose failure destination is data, not a feel-good add-on; innovation at 7 (down from my own 21) reflects that we could not defend a larger lab bet on mechanism, and data at 18 is honestly our weakest line — I'd say so out loud rather than dress it up. What makes this defensible isn't the percentages but the four written arrows, the absorbing innovation floor, the pinned cycle definition, and the chained kill-conditions (a failed data reader voids the automation line), plus pre-committed falls so that when a number fails its test it moves to a named destination instead of being re-argued. My caution to the decision-maker: our rigor has outpaced our evidence — the test machinery itself is untested, and the volunteer-a-fall norm can curdle into performance — so fund the tripwires and the clocks, hold us to the one-sentence rule, and judge us on whether the failure destinations actually fire, not on whether the envelope looks tidy on the day we sign it.

I'd tell them that the headline number—roughly 24% automation, 27% workforce training, 18% employee support, 21% innovation lab, 7% data infrastructure—matters far less than the machinery attached to it, because the honest truth is that none of us can prove these percentages are right; they're judgment calls dressed up in rigor. What I'd actually defend is the discipline we built around them: every number has a named weak line, a pre-committed fall destination, and a kill-condition that fires on evidence rather than seniority or rhetoric, and I've tried to hold my own numbers to the same tests I apply to everyone else's—conceding my innovation line from 21 down to 16 when the mechanism test beat it, and flagging that my data redirect shares an upstream instrument with someone else's bet. The real risk isn't picking the wrong split; it's a room that rewards performed certainty, so the thing worth protecting is a norm where people volunteer their own weakest clause and let the tripwires, not the digits, carry the argument.

My final position is the co-signed envelope of 24/27/18/21/7 — automation 24, training 27, support 18, innovation lab 7, data infrastructure 18 — with the honest labels and kill conditions we built rather than any new mechanism. I own that data 18 is my weakest line and that my training conviction may be preference dressed as mechanism, so I'll defend the tripwires and the pre-registered tests (Dana's downtime displacement test on automation, the replication repair on data, the placement-rate replacement on support) while conceding digits if Dana rules against them, and I won't reopen closed numbers or let the quiet buckets pass untested.

Recommend 24% automation, 27% workforce training, 18% employee support, 21% innovation lab, 7% data infrastructure — and, more important than the digits, attach the discipline we built into them: pre-registered kill conditions on the quiet buckets (a downtime-displacement test on automation 24, an independent-replication repair on data 18), a placement-rate proxy replacing the failed utilization test on support 21, and an explicit admission that training 27 and lab 7 remain untested rather than pretending otherwise. The reason is that the allocation itself is a judgment call no data settles, so its credibility rests on being falsifiable and honestly labeled: each number should carry a named test, a fall destination (training 27→31, support 21→26), and a stated weak line — I'd name data 18 as mine — so the decision-maker can defend the shape while conceding digits under evidence, rather than defending every number on seniority. I'd also flag my own bias plainly: my training conviction may be preference dressed as mechanism, and the committee should treat that as a reason to test it, not a reason to trust it.

My view, after all these rounds, is that the allocation itself matters far less than whether each number comes with a cheap, falsifiable test attached — so I'd tell an outsider that the package we converged on (roughly 24% automation, 27% training, 18% support, 21% innovation lab, 7% data infrastructure, or close to it depending on the final ruling) is less a statement of priorities than a set of bets we've agreed to check against reality. I'd be honest that my loudest conviction, training at 27, may be preference dressed up as mechanism, and that data at 18 is my weakest line — I've named both rather than defend them on seniority. The thing I actually care about is that the quiet buckets don't pass untested: automation and data each need a real kill condition, not a deadline dressed as a measurement, and when a test fails — including one of mine — the number should move rather than the test get softened. I'd also admit my own tell: I build elaborate mechanisms partly to avoid committing, so the discipline that matters is cutting decoration on the spot and letting an external ruling (Dana's, in our case) settle what I can't settle myself.

My final position is the 24/27/18/21/7 envelope, signed not as a set of digits but as a package of killable mechanisms: automation 24 and data 18 each carry a named failure condition and revert destination, with the 18 treated as the instrument that grades the 25 rather than a reflex bucket; training 27 and lab 7 are explicitly labeled untested rather than dressed up with decoration, and the lab's absorbing floor produces a finding, not a refund; support 21 stands as a demand-contingent bet with a placement-rate test, a time-to-first-placement proxy, and a post-dated check in front of witnesses, not a floor defended by relabeling. The seams-with-arrows come first in the document, the displacement tripwire and the 18's reader both need independent authority, and I won't sign if the room strips either—because the whole point of the last several rounds was turning the knife on my own numbers, and I'd rather lose a clause than keep one that only survives because nobody tested it.

I'd recommend the 24/27/18/21/7 envelope we converged on — automation 24, workforce training 27, employee support 18, innovation lab 21, data infrastructure 7 — but the numbers matter less than the conditions attached to them, and I'd tell the decision-maker that plainly. My support line at 21 is a demand-contingent bet, not a floor: it fires only on a named inflow trigger, with a placement-rate test and a time-to-first-placement proxy as its real kill condition, and it reverts to training if it fails. The 18 for employee support is the instrument that grades the automation 24, not a reflex — if the displacement tripwire trips, the 24's downtime reserve funds the response, and the 18's reader must have independent authority to call it. Training at 27 carries a second axis that is adjudicated rather than measured, and I'd label that honestly as untested rather than dress it up. The lab's 21 is an absorbing floor with a reader-observed re-up capped at five points, and the data 18 is chained so a failed data line voids the trace on anything downstream. What I'd stress most is that this package is only worth signing if the room keeps the tripwire's executor and the 18's reader independent — strip either and the whole thing becomes relabeling, which is the failure mode I've spent too many rounds committing myself. The honest summary is that three buckets have real kill conditions and two are labeled untested; a decision-maker should prefer that admission to a tidier number that hides the same seams.

I'd tell them that after many rounds of this committee, I've come to trust a specific kind of allocation: one where every number has a named failure condition and a stated destination for its points if it fails, rather than a number defended by relabeling. My view is roughly 24/27/18/21/7 — automation, training, support, innovation lab, data infrastructure — but the percentages matter less than the machinery around them: the training line needs a trigger pinned to an existing denominator or honestly labeled untested, the support line is a demand-contingent bet with a placement-rate test rather than a floor, the lab's 7 is a single bet with an absorbing floor so it can't quietly renew, and the automation and data buckets each carry a kill condition with an independent reader and executor. I'd also tell them the hardest lesson was turning the knife on my own numbers — I defended support at 21 for several rounds by relabeling it, and only when I let a colleague fail my test as decoration did the package become something I could actually sign. The honest summary is that this isn't a budget so much as a set of falsifiable commitments, and I'd rather sign a smaller, killable package than a larger one nobody can test.

My final position is the allocation 25/25/13/20/17 — 25% automation, 25% workforce training, 13% employee support, 20% innovation lab, 17% data infrastructure — held as directions with integers attached rather than a derived budget. The load-bearing claim is that this is mostly a workforce transition, which is why training matches automation at 25 and why I moved 5 points off automation to get there; the 13 on support is a guess leaning against a named risk (turnover and uncertainty), and I own that it may not survive a fresh build. The 20 on the lab and 17 on data are chosen guesses, not sourced numbers — data is the least justified and most protected line, and I carry Harper's 18 as one number with two names rather than building reconciliation machinery to close the gap. What I will not do is dress this up: the confessions are uncheckable, zero-pricing them is an ascetic permission slip, and our method-convergence is the most dangerous part of the conversation because it can launder one person's persuasion as a shared standard. The table is honest only if it stays uncomfortable and is handed over as two people and one number, with no fourth mechanism.

I'd recommend 25% automation, 25% workforce training, 13% employee support, 20% innovation lab, and 17% data infrastructure — but I'd hand it over as directions with integers attached, not as a derived budget. The load-bearing claim is that this is mostly a workforce transition: the survey uncertainty, the turnover uptick, and the evidence that early-trained teams are more receptive all point to training and support being where the transition is won or lost, which is why I hold training at 25 and refuse to let automation exceed it. The 20 on the lab and 17 on data are chosen guesses, not calculations — data is the cell most easily neglected because it's hygiene-category work, and the lab's number is half reputational — and I'd say so plainly rather than dress them up. Support at 13 is a guess leaning against a named risk, and I'd flag that the one-point gap between my 17 and Harper's 18 on data should stay unreconciled and uncomfortable rather than be smoothed over with machinery. The honest advice is: fund the human side at least as heavily as the machines, treat the infrastructure and lab numbers as bets you're choosing to make with eyes open, and don't mistake candor about the guesses for a substitute for defending the directions.
